item.title: The Tower: Parts, Pot, and Pump
item.description:
Notes from the Vertical Garden: Large Hydroponic Vegetable Tower (archive) page on MakerWorld, designed by Structales (released 2025-04-21). Summarized from a PDF printout of the page; the filament list at the page break and the video were not captured. Check the model page for anything you are about to buy or print.

At a glance

Type Pump-fed “rain” tower: pump in a sealed pot, 20 mm center pipe, sprinkler at the top
Height Up to 180 cm with all three pot sizes stacked
Footprint Pot 38 × 38 cm (printed lid 36.8 cm square)
Pot sizes GrowBig4 (large crops), Grow8 (radishes, small salad), GrowSmall4 (head lettuce, herbs, flowers); each big pot is about 18 × 18 × 20 cm
Print time Main tower profile: 72 h over 14 plates (P1S shown). Optional support rings: 15 h, 6 plates. Alternatives and options: 41.5 h, 4 plates
Filament Lots of it. Designer: use PETG, smooth plate recommended
Track record Tested outdoors for 5 months, wind-resistant per the designer

What to buy besides the printed parts

From the designer’s list:

  • A large plant pot, at least 40 L / 10 gal, square, thick upper rim, no drainage holes, plastic (preferably polyethylene), with a drillable rim. The model is sized for a 38 × 38 × 40 cm pot; the page lists several European planters and notes the lid’s STEP files can be adapted. A commenter points out you can screw the lid to a board and cut it to fit any pot. The designer says a 5-gallon bucket is too small. See Tower Sourcing in the USA for pots that worked.
  • A submersible pump. The designer uses a Sicce Syncra Silent 2.0 (the 1.5 should also work). Another commenter designed a connector for a cheaper Amazon pump (MakerWorld model 1625658).
  • 20 mm outer-diameter sturdy pipe, 2 m, cut to length (designer used aluminum; one commenter used stainless). In the US see Tower Sourcing in the USA for 3/4" OD options.
  • About 28 × M4 countersunk screws, 16 mm, with nuts; 2 × shorter M4 countersunk, 8 mm, for the filter flap.
  • 12 × M5 screws and nuts for the base lid. Nuts go into the grow pots too: 4 per big pot and 2 per small pot.
  • 3 cm aquarium foam, cut into a filter pad for the lid.
  • Net pots for the plants. One commenter notes that nuts can get stuck, and suggests embedded nuts instead.

The designer’s growing setup: Terra Aquatica TriPart fertilizers, a pH meter and EC meter, filtered or rain water, rockwool cubes with vermiculite on top, then clay pebbles in the net pot after the roots develop.

Assembly order, in short

The designer says don’t use an electric screwdriver or overtighten: it cracks the printed and plastic parts.

  1. Base — screw together the base lid parts (12 M5 screws and nuts), put the pump in the pot, and make sure the pump output sits dead center in the pot (measure it).
  2. Lid and filter — route the cable through the square hole; drill two holes on each side of the pot to line up with the lid (they hold the rods); nuts in the small holes; foam filter with a center hole and a slit facing away from the filter flap.
  3. Structure — the 2 m pipe goes in the center and must line up with the pump outlet; two rods go through pot and base; fill remaining lid holes with the cover parts; put the GrowBig4 on top.
  4. Final — stack the pots, then the black sprinkler on top.
  5. Test — fill the pot halfway. If no water comes out the top, the pump is too weak or the pump-to-pipe connection leaks (add a sealing ring). Screw the grow pots to each other, then fit the lids. If the water gets too warm, use the white cap on the top; take it off on colder days to warm the water.

To clean the pot, remove the top lids, pull the two base rods, and lift the whole tower aside so the pipe slides out; the plants stay in place.

What commenters found

  • Algae at seams. Each level snaps together, and one commenter got algae from water seeping at the seams, so they printed a cover that snaps inside to hide it. The designer says their own tower ran two months indoors on parquet without a spill.
  • Leak at the pump diaphragm. One builder found the diaphragm isn’t airtight and sealed it with gaffer tape.
  • Print problems. A builder had trouble at the grow pot’s connector; the designer says to use the “BigTower with connector supports” print profile.
  • Water temperature. A commenter running two towers reports the high flow rate keeps the water temperature stable even in high ambient heat.
  • Add-ons. A TPU cover cap for the plant holes (MakerWorld model 1526313) and a “Hydroponic tower light kit” from another designer.

Implications for the garage

  • Pump: the 180 cm tower needs a pump with enough head to push water 2 m up. Pick by max lift, and don’t assume a cheap pump has it; see the shopping list.
  • Reservoir heat: the sealed pot is a good place for a 50 W aquarium heater, and the white cap stays off in winter per the designer.
  • Freeze risk: the pot’s water is insulated by the lid, but the 20 mm pipe, pots, and net cups are full of water in cold air. Drain the pipe before a hard freeze.
  • Light: 180 cm of tower needs lights along its whole height; see Garage Grow Setup.

item.title: Tower Sourcing in the USA: Pot and Center Pipe
item.description:
The tower is designed around European parts: a 38 × 38 × 40 cm square planter and a 20 mm OD center pipe. Neither is easy to find in the US. This page collects what builders in the MakerWorld comments (about 1,200 ratings; read through 2026-11-12) actually used, plus my own sizing checks. Claims are marked (commenter) where a builder reported them, and (calc) where I worked them out from standard sizes. Nothing here has been built or tested by me yet.

Center pipe (20 mm OD)

The pipe carries water up the middle and, per the designer, also adds stability. It runs through a 20 mm bore in every module, so anything that sticks out past the OD will not pass: no welds, rivets, or external couplers.

What commenters used

Pipe Fit Source
20 mm aluminum Designer’s choice; third season, still looks fine Designer
20 mm stainless Works Commenter
3/4" OD vinyl tubing 19.05 mm, “worked perfectly” Commenter
1/2" PEX Used as the center pipe once; mostly used for the 16 mm ring uprights (see below) Commenters
16 mm aluminum plus a printed 20→16 reducer at the pump Works but is “a snug fit”; how the 16 mm pipe is centered in a 20 mm bore is not explained Commenter
16/22 aquarium tubing One builder says it fits; another says it does not (22 mm OD in a 20 mm hole). Treat as not working Commenters

Standard US sizes against the 20 mm bore (calc)

Stock OD vs 20 mm
3/4" OD tube (aluminum, stainless, vinyl) 19.05 mm 0.95 mm under; slides through, a little play
1/2" PEX 15.9 mm 4 mm under; needs a shim or sleeve
1/2" PVC / CPVC 21.3 mm 1.3 mm over; needs shaving (a commenter did not want to)
3/4" PEX 22.2 mm Over

So 3/4" OD tube is the closest US match. A metric 20 mm tube from a supplier such as McMaster-Carr is another route, but I have not checked stock.

The aluminum tubes I am considering

Two 3/4" OD, 6 ft candidates. The Everbilt tube is the better fit: its thinner wall leaves a 16.6 mm ID, about 70% more flow area than the Grainger tube’s 12.7 mm ID (calc), and it is close to the roughly 17 mm ID of a 20 × 1.5 mm tube.

Everbilt (Home Depot) Grainger 795AP1
OD 0.750 in (19.05 mm) 0.750 in (19.05 mm)
Wall 0.0489 in (1.24 mm) 0.125 in (3.2 mm)
ID 0.652 in (16.6 mm) (calc) 0.500 in (12.7 mm)
Alloy Not stated on the listing 6061-T6, extruded
Length 6 ft (3 ft and 4 ft also sold) 6 ft

Everbilt 3/4 in x 6 ft aluminum round tube (archive): specs from a screenshot of the listing (retail page, in stock for store pickup on 2026-11-12). Measure the real OD with calipers; the thinner wall is more flexible, so handle it carefully.

Grainger 6061 aluminum round tube, item 795AP1 (archive):
Material 6061-T6, extruded
OD 3/4 in (19.05 mm)
Wall 0.125 in (3.2 mm)
ID 0.5 in (12.7 mm)
Length 6 ft (183 cm)

Spec as shown on the listing; check the current page before ordering.

  • Length: a single 6 ft piece means no joint. The designer’s 180 cm tower includes the pot and the pipe stops 1 cm above the Rainbase, so 183 cm should just do it. Add up your module heights first; a taller build will not fit.
  • OD: 0.95 mm under the bore. Take up the slack at the pump connector with PTFE tape or heat shrink, or print a connector with a 19.05 mm bore. A loose connector is where leaks start (the designer’s fix for leaks there is a sealing ring).
  • ID: the Grainger tube’s 12.7 mm gives roughly 45% less flow area than a 20 × 1.5 mm tube (about 17 mm ID; the designer’s wall thickness is not stated) (calc); the Everbilt’s 16.6 mm is nearly the same as that tube. It matters because the pump has to lift water about 1.8 m. Check the pump’s maximum head against the finished tower height before relying on it; I have not verified the Syncra’s head rating.

If you have to join shorter lengths

Use an internal sleeve: a tube that slides inside both ends, 4 to 6 in long, scuffed, degreased, and bonded with two-part epoxy, with the sections butted tight. Welding thin aluminum tube needs TIG and leaves a bead that must be ground flush. Rivets and screws leave heads that snag in the modules. With the Everbilt tube (16.6 mm ID) a 5/8" OD (15.9 mm) sleeve leaves about 0.7 mm of clearance for epoxy. The Grainger tube’s 12.7 mm ID is too small for that, so with it just buy the 6 ft length.

Epoxy and food safety

Cured epoxy is generally inert, but look for NSF/ANSI 61 (drinking-water components) or FDA 21 CFR 175.300 compliance on the datasheet for the exact product. Avoid metal-filled putties. Wipe out squeeze-out so no bead is exposed to flowing water, mix at the stated ratio, cure fully (often 24 h or more), and flush the system with plain water before planting. An epoxy-free alternative is a tight press-fit sleeve sealed with 100% silicone sold as aquarium-safe (bathroom silicone often contains mildewcide).

Aluminum in nutrient solution

One commenter worried aluminum reacts with fertilizer salts at pH 5 to 6.5 and suggested PVC-U or polyethylene. The designer found no evidence against aluminum online and is in their third season with it. Someone else planned a polyethylene pipe (cheap, easy to cut, 10 m coil). If it bothers you, choose stainless or plastic.

Ring uprights (optional support structure)

The “Rings V4” print profile needs four 1 m uprights of 16 mm OD pipe. In the US, 1/2" PEX works (15.9 mm). One builder put a 7/16" wooden dowel inside the PEX to stiffen it. Copper also fits but is expensive. In Europe the part is sold as “rigid M16 installation pipe”.

Pump

Commenters used the Sicce Syncra Silent 2.0 (designer’s pick), a 700 GPH “WUCIOOO” pump, and a 40 W, 3000 L/h pump. The pump I plan to use:

VIVOSUN 660GPH submersible pump, size 6"×4"-660 (archive), from a screenshot of the listing on 2026-11-12:
Flow 660 GPH (2500 L/h), at zero lift
Max lift 8.2 ft (2.5 m)
Power 35 W
Price $19.99
Extras Adjustable flow, three barbed adapters, suction-cup feet, detachable body
  • Lift margin: the tower needs about 1.8 m of lift, 72% of the pump’s max head, so about 0.7 m of margin at shutoff (calc). Actual flow at 1.8 m will be well below 660 GPH, and the pipe’s friction takes more. Test it half full as the designer advises and use the flow adjuster if it sprays too hard.
  • Outlet adapters: three threaded barbs come in the box, 0.5", 0.62" and 0.75". None fits inside the 16.6 mm ID pipe, because barb ridges are wider than the nominal size. Use the 0.75" barb with a 2 to 3 in piece of 3/4" ID flexible tube, clamped on the barb, with the pipe pushed into the other end. The tube’s OD (about 1 in) does not matter because the joint sits below the lid. Do not clamp the pipe end: the pipe has to slide out for cleaning. The flexible tube also forgives a pump that is slightly off-center, but the outlet should still be near dead center under the pipe. Use the 0.62" or 0.5" barbs only to throttle flow; their bore sizes are not stated.
  • Cord: it has a molded plug. Check it fits through the lid’s square cable hole before assembly.

Pot (reservoir)

The designer’s requirements: at least 40 L (10 gal), square, thick upper rim, no drain holes, plastic (polyethylene preferred), drillable rim. The footprint is about 38 × 38 cm.

Option Reported by Notes
27-gal storage tote, cut a hole in the lid Commenter (BJ’s tote) “Works perfectly.” Wider base. Two builders used it.
Two 27-gal totes under a plywood top Commenter (4 towers, 2 reservoirs) Spray-painted the black totes white against heat. Got leaks between layers and at the board; plans silicone between each layer. Plants got crowded at two towers per 4 ft.
Plywood board between base and any pot Designer-endorsed (highest-liked tip, 39) Screw the round or square base to a board, then adapt the board to the pot. One builder clamped it with a gasket.
Step2 Lakewood planter box Three commenters Needs a modified base (STEP and STL shared by commenters in Google Drive). It is a self-watering planter; the inner basin cannot be removed, so usable volume is less. One builder refills about every 2 weeks at two 15-minute waterings a day. Hold the base plates carefully; they are tight against the rings.
Allen + Roth 14 in self-watering planter (Lowe’s) Commenter Extended the base edges by a few mm; no leaks.
Tusco MSQT23BK square planter (Amazon) Commenter Reported only as purchased.
IKEA Sortera 60 L Several EU builders Needs printed adapter parts (MakerWorld model 1594718). A high-tensile pipe was added to carry weight. I have not confirmed the US IKEA sells it.

Avoid:

  • 5-gallon buckets. The designer says that is too small for a tower this size, and one builder who adapted a thin square pot said the sides bulged when it filled.
  • Galvanized steel cans. Suggested once in the thread; they would rust in nutrient solution.
  • Thin-walled planters. One builder found a planter weak where the tower mounts.

Reservoir size matters. One builder says a 40+ L pot lasts about 4 days in summer if filled to the top; another lost track of pH and had to change the water repeatedly.

Build and print gotchas from the comments

  • Weak tabs. The joiner tabs on the main body break during printing or later (several builders). Printing with the BigTower with connector supports profile helps. Updated V5 profile moves the seam to the middle and slows the speed.
  • Feet failing on GrowSmall4 and Grow8. The bottom right foot fails on some printers (P2S reports). Changing the seam to random fixed one; adding hand-placed supports fixed another.
  • Wet PETG. Dry PETG first, even new rolls. Several builders say that fixed their failures.
  • Print bed. The rings do not fit on a 220 × 220 mm bed (K1C); the rest does.
  • Filter flap leaks. Too thick a foam pad caused it for one builder (thinner pad fixed it). Others used sealing tape, or a U-shaped TPU gasket (a flat 0.6 mm gasket made it worse). A “no flap” base option exists in the print profiles.
  • Missing a Big4 pot. The Grow8 pot with four top connectors has no offset, so with one fewer Big4 pot the rings will not attach (one builder hit this at 2 m tall).
  • Nuts stuck. An M5 nut jammed and blocked disassembly; embedded or heat-set nuts are suggested.
  • Layer leaks. Silicone or a seal at each seam if you mount the base to a board (see the four-tower build above).
  • Top rain module arms failed repeatedly for one P1S owner; the designer asks about brims and infill (use grid, crosshatch or gyroid, not something sparse).

Growing notes from the comments

  • A builder grew 72 strawberries in one tower; high flow also kept water temperature stable in heat.
  • Another runs EC at 1800 to 2200 for fruiting crops. Lettuce and herbs need much lower.
  • Rockwool starts, with clay pebbles in the net pot, per the designer. Clay can skew EC and pH readings, and one builder asked for printed inserts instead.
  • Several people added lights: LEDs built into the support rings, or a taller lid. Files are on other MakerWorld pages (one linked at the designer’s invitation).
  • PETG is fine in water, and white PETG reflects sun but encourages algae; the top parts are black for that reason.
  • Existing commercial towers: one builder scaled the model to 86% so their mesh pots and clips fit.

Shopping check before you buy

  • Pot is square, 10+ gal, no drain holes, drillable rim, or you have a board to adapt it
  • Pump max head is above tower height plus the extra loss from a narrower pipe
  • Center pipe OD is within about 1 mm under 20 mm and has a way to seal at the pump
  • Pump connector matches the pipe OD (printed connector in the print profiles)
  • Epoxy, if used, has an NSF 61 or FDA 21 CFR 175.300 datasheet
  • PETG is dry before printing

Open questions

  • Real flow of the VIVOSUN 660 at 1.8 m lift through the 16.6 mm ID Everbilt pipe (or 12.7 mm ID Grainger), and whether the lift is enough to reach the sprinkler.
  • Whether the 3/4" ID tube grips the 19.05 mm pipe snugly enough to seal without a clamp; pot depth minus pump height sets the pipe length and the joint length, so dry fit first.
  • Whether the VIVOSUN plug fits the lid’s cable hole.
  • Alloy of the Everbilt tube (not stated on the listing).
  • Whether the printed pump connector can be re-sized for a 19.05 mm pipe, or whether tape is enough.
  • Which US pot to use. The 27-gal tote and a plywood adapter is the most reported without custom CAD.

item.title: Hydroponics 101
item.description:
The short version of what a vertical tower needs: water + dissolved nutrients, oxygen at the roots, light, and a stable temperature. Everything else is detail.

How a vertical tower works

The tower in these notes (see The Tower) has a submersible pump in a 40+ L pot at the base. The pump pushes solution up a 20 mm center pipe to a sprinkler head at the top, and it rains down through the stack of grow pots, past the roots of plants held in net cups, and drains back through the pot floors into the reservoir. Roots get water, air, and a shallow standing layer in each pot between cycles; one commenter on the model found roots look healthier this way than in designs that drain dry.

A bigger reservoir is more forgiving: pH and nutrient concentration drift more slowly. This design’s 40+ L pot is a good size.

How often to run the pump

The model page gives no pump schedule, and the designer calls the system low-maintenance, so treat these as starting points borrowed from university-extension trickle towers, then adjust by watching the roots:

Stage Pump schedule (lights on) Notes
Seedlings just transplanted 15 min on / 15 min off Roots are short; keep them damp
Established plants 15 min on / 30–45 min off Cut back if the cups stay soggy or algae shows
Lights off Keep cycling, e.g. 15 min on / 45 off Don’t leave a trickle tower dry overnight; the pump runs 24 h on its own timer, separate from the light timer

Use a plain mechanical or digital outlet timer. Watch the roots, not the clock: white and fuzzy is healthy; slimy, brown, or smelling bad means too wet, too warm, or too little oxygen. Wilting at midday with a dry cup means run it more often.

A pump that fails while the lights are on can kill a tower in hours, so check it the first thing every day.

Feeding: pH and EC

  • pH — keep the solution at 5.5–6.5 (aim ~5.8–6.0). Outside that range, plants cannot take up some nutrients even though they are in the water.
  • EC (electrical conductivity, how strong the nutrient mix is) — the one number that tells you when to add nutrients. Measured in mS/cm.
Crop group pH EC (mS/cm)
Lettuce, arugula, bok choy 5.5–6.5 1.2–1.6
Basil, other herbs 5.5–6.5 1.0–1.6
Kale, chard 5.5–6.5 1.2–2.0 (the same solution as lettuce works)
Strawberries 5.5–6.2 1.8–2.2
Dwarf tomatoes 5.8–6.3 2.0–4.0
Peppers 5.8–6.3 lower than tomatoes, roughly 0.8–1.8

Start seedlings at roughly a quarter to half strength and work up. (Commercial growers feed seedlings at full strength; weak is the cautious choice for a first run.)

Routine for a small tower:

  1. Daily — look at the tank level and the roots. Top off with plain water (plants drink water faster than nutrients, so topping off with plain water keeps EC from creeping up).
  2. Daily for the first few weeks, then every 2–3 days once readings are stable — check pH and EC at the same time of day. Adjust pH after measuring EC. Adjust pH with small doses of pH-down (or up); add nutrients if EC has dropped below target.
  3. Every 2 weeks — drain, rinse, and refill the whole reservoir with fresh solution. Top-offs cannot fix an unbalanced mix.
  4. As needed — wipe slime off the pump intake and any drip points.

Use a complete hydroponic nutrient (two- or three-part) rather than garden fertilizer, and follow its label for the dilution. Miracle-Gro and similar lawn-and-garden products are not formulated for this.

Water temperature (important in a garage)

Keep the reservoir around 68–72 °F; treat 75 °F as the ceiling. Warmer water encourages root rot (often Pythium) and holds less oxygen; much colder water slows growth. In an unheated garage in winter, the problem is cold, not hot — see Garage Grow Setup.

Good first crops

Crop Why it works Roughly seed to first harvest
Loose-leaf and butterhead lettuce Fast, low EC, tolerates cool temperatures; cut-and-come-again 5–8 weeks
Basil Loves the tower, lots of leaf; needs warmth 5–7 weeks
Arugula, bok choy Fast and forgiving 4–6 weeks
Kale, Swiss chard Cold tolerant; good for a cool garage 6–8 weeks
Mint, parsley, cilantro Mint grows like a weed (give it its own spot); cilantro bolts quickly 6–10 weeks
Strawberries (day-neutral) A reasonable second project; buy bare-root crowns, not seed months

The tower is built for more (the designer lists tomatoes, cucumbers, broccoli, kohlrabi, peppers, and eggplant, with an optional ring support for heavy crops) and offers three pot sizes: GrowBig4 for large crops, Grow8 for radishes and small salad, GrowSmall4 for head lettuce, herbs, and flowers. For a first winter in a garage, fill it with the leafy crops above: fruiting crops need much stronger light and more heat than a winter garage gives them. Dwarf cherry tomatoes and peppers are a step-two project once the routine is working.

Common problems

Symptom Likely cause
Pale new leaves pH out of range, or EC too low
Brown, slimy roots Water too warm or low dissolved oxygen (root rot, often Pythium)
Brown leaf tips on lettuce Usually a calcium-delivery problem from fast growth under strong light with poor airflow: add a fan and ease the light. Very high EC causes a different, general leaf-edge burn
Algae in the tank or on the cups Light reaching the solution; cover the tank and use opaque parts
Tall, floppy plants Light too weak or too far away
Lettuce bolting (flower stalk) Heat or very long days

Safety

Water and mains power share a space. Plug everything into a GFCI-protected outlet, use drip loops on cords, and keep power strips and timers well above the reservoir.

item.title: Seed Starting for Hydroponics
item.description:
Seeds start in a small plug of growing medium, under light, then the whole plug drops into a net cup in the tower. No soil is involved.

Mediums

Medium Notes
Rockwool cubes (1″) Cheap, standard. Needs a pre-soak: saturate in nutrient solution at pH ~5.5 until the air bubbles stop (a few minutes), drain, and don’t squeeze. Wear gloves and avoid breathing the dust; the fibers irritate skin.
Rapid Rooter / peat-based plugs Easy, no pre-soak pH step; pop the seed in and keep moist
Coco coir plugs Good water retention; rinse if not pre-buffered
Oasis cubes Foam; works but holds a lot of water

For a first try, rockwool or plugs are the least fiddly. Whichever you pick, it has to fit the tower’s net cups.

Step by step

  1. Soak the plug in pH ~5.5 solution and let the excess drain. It should be damp, not dripping.
  2. Sow 1–2 seeds per hole (3 for tiny seeds like lettuce, thinned later). Do not bury light-dependent seeds such as lettuce; barely cover them.
  3. Cover the tray with a clear humidity dome until the seeds sprout.
  4. Warm — most crops want 65–75 °F at the plug. In a cold garage, a seedling heat mat under the tray does more good than a space heater. Lettuce germinates poorly above ~80 °F; peppers and basil like it warmer.
  5. Light as soon as they sprout — take the dome off and put a light a few inches above the seedlings, 14–16 hours a day. Raise it as they grow. Too far away means stretched, leggy seedlings.
  6. Water from below — keep an inch of very weak nutrient solution (a quarter of the label strength, EC ~0.4–0.8) in the bottom of the tray. Do not let the plugs dry out.
  7. Transplant into the tower when roots show out of the bottom of the plug and the seedling has 2–3 true leaves (not counting the first pair), usually 2–3 weeks for lettuce and herbs (longer under dim light).

Germination quick reference

Crop Germination temp Days to sprout
Lettuce 60–70 °F 2–7
Arugula, bok choy 60–75 °F 3–7
Kale, chard 60–75 °F 4–10
Basil 65–75 °F (best ~70) 5–10
Cilantro 60–70 °F 7–21
Parsley 65–80 °F 12–21+
Peppers 80–85 °F 7–14
Tomatoes 70–80 °F 5–10

Staggering

Sow a few new plugs every 1–2 weeks. A tower planted all at once gives one big harvest and then nothing; staggered sowing gives a steady supply, and a spare seedling ready when a plant fails.

Troubleshooting

  • Nothing sprouts — too cold, too dry, or old seed. Check the plug is damp and the temperature is within the range above, ideally mid-range.
  • White fuzz or mold on the plug — too wet and too still. Vent the dome and lower the moisture.
  • Seedlings fall over at the base — damping off, usually from wet, cool, stagnant conditions. Add airflow (a small fan on low) and let the surface dry a bit.
  • Leggy seedlings — light too far or too weak.

item.title: Garage Grow Setup
item.description:
A winter garage changes three things: there is no sunlight, it is cold, and there is moisture around electricity. All three have fixes.

Light

Garage windows will not do it. Plants need a dedicated light.

  • Seedlings: roughly 100–200 µmol/m²/s (PPFD) at the canopy, 14–16 h/day.
  • Leafy greens and herbs in the tower: roughly 200–400 µmol/m²/s, 14–16 h/day.
  • Fruiting crops (tomatoes, peppers, strawberries): considerably more, 400+ (a rule of thumb; not checked against a source).

A light delivering ~300 µmol/m²/s for 16 h works out to a daily light integral of about 17 mol/m²/day, a good target for lettuce. Without good airflow, aim a little lower (13–14) to avoid tip burn.

The tower stands up to 180 cm (about 6 ft) with all three pot sizes stacked, so you want light that covers its height, not just the top. A 1 m bar covers roughly half of a full-height column; use two per side, or build the tower shorter. A commenter built LED strips into the optional support rings. Options:

  • Full-spectrum LED bars or strips mounted vertically alongside the tower, one per side. This is usually the best fit.
  • Full-spectrum LED panel or bar above the seedling tray for the starting area.
  • T5 high-output fluorescents — work well for seedlings, cheaper but bulkier and less efficient.

Look for a manufacturer-stated PPFD (or PAR) figure at a stated distance, not just “equivalent to 1000 W” claims. Give the light its own timer (14–16 h on). The pump runs its interval cycle around the clock on a separate timer.

Heat

Unheated garage lows will drop the reservoir towards freezing, which stops growth and can split pumps and fittings.

  1. Insulate — wrap or place the reservoir in foam board or a cooler-style enclosure; keep it off the cold concrete floor on a pallet or foam.
  2. Aquarium heater (adjustable) in the reservoir, set about 68 °F, plugged into a GFCI. This is the single most useful heat item. It must stay fully submerged: a heater exposed by a falling water level gets very hot very fast.
  3. Freeze protection for everything else — the reservoir heater only protects the tank. The tower column, tubing, net-cup roots, and pump all sit in garage air. If the forecast is near 32 °F, bring the tower inside or drain the column and lines, and keep the plants somewhere warm.
  4. Room-level heat — insulation plus the reservoir heater is the preferred plan. If you add an electric space heater, plug it directly into a wall outlet (never a power strip or extension cord), keep 3 ft of clearance, use one with tip-over shutoff, and don’t leave it running unattended; NFPA advises unplugging it when you leave. No fuel-burning heaters in the garage (carbon monoxide), and keep fuels and solvents away from any heater.
  5. Seedling heat mat with a thermostat for germination.

Timers and power

  • A timer for the lights (14–16 h on) and a separate timer for the pump (15 min on, 15–45 off, around the clock) so the schedules are independent.
  • GFCI outlet or GFCI adapter — not optional.
  • Surge-protected power strip mounted above the water line (for the lights and timers, not for a heater).
  • Low-water protection — as the tank drops, the pump can run dry (which damages it) and the heater can end up in air. Check the level daily; a float switch or low-water cutoff is cheap insurance.

Meters and supplies

  • pH meter (digital pen type) with calibration solution (pH 4 and 7); calibrate regularly and store as directed. Cheap pH test drops or strips work for rough checks only.
  • EC meter — buy EC, not just TDS. TDS is calculated from EC with a 0.5 or 0.7 factor, so ppm readings from different meters don’t match.
  • pH Down (and pH Up) — small bottles last a long time.
  • Complete hydroponic nutrient — a two- or three-part set designed for leafy greens.
  • Seed-starting tray, humidity dome, heat mat, rockwool or plugs — see Seed Starting.
  • Small clip-on fan for airflow. Seedlings need it, and grown lettuce needs it too to prevent tip burn and damp mold, especially in a closed tent.
  • Measuring syringes or a graduated cylinder for doses.
  • Opaque tubing and a lid on the reservoir to keep out light and algae. Print or paint the tower parts opaque too (check the model for PETG vs PLA; PETG copes better with a cold, wet garage).

Water and mixing

  • Know your tap water. Check your utility’s water-quality report. Very soft water (Asheville’s runs about 24 ppm alkalinity) starts near zero EC and has little pH buffering, so pH swings fast, and some nutrient formulas need a Cal-Mag supplement. Chlorine is fine; chloramine is not removed by letting water sit. Well water needs a water analysis first.
  • Mixing: add each nutrient part to the water separately and stir; never combine the concentrates. Measure EC first, then adjust pH. pH Down is acid: wear gloves and eye protection.
